Main Deities * '''{{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi}}''' (伊弉諾尊) * '''{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami}}''' (伊弉册尊) ; Enshrined Deities * {{ill|Zōka Sanshin|ja|造化三神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zōka Sanshin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 別天津神|1=Kotoamatsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q776371}} – {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|WD=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi}}, {{ill|Takami-Musubi|ja|高御産巣日神|1=Takamimusubi|WD=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タカミムスビ}}, and {{ill|Kami-Musubi|ja|神産巣日神|1=Kamimusubi|WD=Q3275901|lt=Kamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カミムスビ}}{{Cite web |title=Ame-no-Minakanushi |url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2038 |website=JapanKnowledge |access-date=2024-12-29 |first=NetAdvance Inc |last=NetAdvance Inc |quote=Takami-Musubi, Kami-Musubi, and Ame-no-Minakanushi are the three gods of creation.}} == History == [[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]] According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|WD=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|Shiraiwa Mountain|ja|白岩山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraiwa Mountain|1=shiroiwayama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579633}}, {{ill|Myōhōgatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhōgatake|1=myouhougatake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|WD=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]. It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|WD=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kannon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 観音菩薩}} at the site. {{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|WD=Q6443450|lt=Kumano}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}. During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. More detailed information on rituals, shrine architecture, and related legends can be found in the full article. == History == === Founding === The shrine's origins trace back to the first century, attributed to the founding by Prince {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto}}, a son of the legendary twelfth emperor of Japan, Keikō. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. panoramio.jpg|alt=三峰神社奥宮鳥居|Torii at the Inner Shrine of Mitsumine, 2011-02-27 == References == {{Izanagi Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{translated page|ja|三峯神社|version=103708866|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{Draft categories| [[simple:User:Mitsumine Shrine]] }} {{everybodywiki link|Mitsumine Shrine}} {{everybodywiki link|Mitsumine Shrine|Mitsumine Shrine}} [[image:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|260px]] [[simple:User:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[ja:三峯神社]] [[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]] [[fr:User:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{Commons category|Mitsumine-jinja}} {{wikidata link|Q11355207}} [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Buildings in Chichibu, Saitama]] [[Category:Everybody linked]] [[Category:everybodywiki import successful]] [[Category:Former Prefectural Shrines in Saitama Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Chichibu, Saitama]] [[Category:Kanto Mountains]] [[Category:Kazan'in family]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]] [[Category:Saitama Prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Sexuality and gender identity-based cultures]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Saitama Prefecture]] [[Category:Shugendō]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru Legend]] [[Category:pages]]

[[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[sn:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=File:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|prefecture={{ill|Chichibu|WD=Q647079|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}|coordinates={{Coord|35.925431|N|138.930397|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}|deity={{ill|Izanagi and Izanami|WD=Q12259961|1=Izanagi and Izanami}}}}'''Mitsumine Shrine''' is a [[Beppyo Shrine]] in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|en|Chichibu, Saitama|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu, Saitama|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =

Setsubun Exorcism Festival ("Gomottomo-sama," {{ill|February 3|en|February 3|WD=Q2315|lt=February 3|1=February 3}}) | map = Japan Saitama }} [[File:Mitsumine Shrine - various scenes - Feb 3 2021.webm|thumb|Mitsumine Shrine]] '''Mitsumine Shrine''' (三峯神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|ja|埼玉県秩父市|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu, Saitama|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[Category:sn_crud|commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=File:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|prefecture={{ill|Chichibu|WD=Q647079|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}|coordinates={{Coord|35.925431|N|138.930397|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}|deity={{ill|Izanagi and Izanami|WD=Q12259961|1=Izanagi and Izanami}}}}'''Mitsumine Shrine''' is a [[Beppyo Shrine]] in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|en|Chichibu, Saitama|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu, Saitama|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =

The shrine worships the {{ill|Japanese wolf|ja|狼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese wolf|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|1=Wolf|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18498}} as a guardian deity[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|WD=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}. == Deities == ; Main Deities * '''{{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi|1=Izanagi}}''' (伊弉諾尊) * '''{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}''' (伊弉册尊) ; Enshrined Deities * {{ill|Zōka Sanshin|ja|造化三神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zōka Sanshin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 別天津神|1=Kotoamatsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q776371}} – {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|WD=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi|1=Ame-no-Minakanushi}}, {{ill|Takami-Musubi|ja|高御産巣日神|1=Takamimusubi|WD=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タカミムスビ}}, and {{ill|Kami-Musubi|ja|神産巣日神|1=Kamimusubi|WD=Q3275901|lt=Kamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カミムスビ}}{{Cite web |title=Ame-no-Minakanushi |url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2038 |website=JapanKnowledge |access-date=2024-12-29 |first=NetAdvance Inc |last=NetAdvance Inc |quote=Takami-Musubi, Kami-Musubi, and Ame-no-Minakanushi are the three gods of creation.}} == History == [[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]] According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|WD=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass|1=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|Shiraiwa Mountain|ja|白岩山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraiwa Mountain|1=shiroiwayama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579633}}, {{ill|Myōhōgatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhōgatake|1=myouhougatake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|WD=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain|1=Mount Kumotori}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]. It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|WD=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Ōshima}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai|1=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kannon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 観音菩薩}} at the site. {{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|WD=Q6443450|lt=Kumano|1=Kumano region}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}. During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =

It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}{{Cite web |title=What is Mitsumine Shrine? |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E5%B3%AF%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE-638822#:~:text=%E3%81%BF%E3%81%A4%E3%81%BF%E3%81%AD%E2%80%90%E3%81%98%E3%82%93%E3%81%98%E3%82%83%E3%80%90%E4%B8%89,%E3%81%91%E3%83%BB%E7%81%AB%E9%99%A4%E3%81%91%E3%81%A8%E3%81%97%E3%81%A6%E6%9C%89%E5%90%8D%E3%80%82 |website=Kotobank |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja |first=Digital Daijisen, Seisenban |last=Japan National Dictionary, Nihon Daihyakka Zensho, Digital Daijisen Plus |publisher=[[DIGITALIO]]}} and is currently listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|WD=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. Together with {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|en|Chichibu Shrine|WD=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine|1=Chichibu Shrine}} and {{ill|Hodosan Shrine|ja|宝登山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hodosan Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寳登山神社}}, it is one of the {{ill|Chichibu Three Shrines|ja|秩父三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135550808|1=Q135550808}}. At the front of the main hall stands a rare {{ill|Mitsu Torii|ja|三ツ鳥居|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsu Torii|1=Mitsutorii|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11354046}}. The shrine worships the {{ill|Japanese wolf|ja|狼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese wolf|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|1=Wolf|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18498}} as a guardian deity[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|WD=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}. == Deities == ; Main Deities * '''{{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi|1=Izanagi}}''' (伊弉諾尊) * '''{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}''' (伊弉册尊) ; Enshrined Deities * {{ill|Zōka Sanshin|ja|造化三神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zōka Sanshin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 別天津神|1=Kotoamatsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q776371}} – {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|WD=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi|1=Ame-no-Minakanushi}}, {{ill|Takami-Musubi|ja|高御産巣日神|1=Takamimusubi|WD=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タカミムスビ}}, and {{ill|Kami-Musubi|ja|神産巣日神|1=Kamimusubi|WD=Q3275901|lt=Kamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カミムスビ}}{{Cite web |title=Ame-no-Minakanushi |url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2038 |website=JapanKnowledge |access-date=2024-12-29 |first=NetAdvance Inc |last=NetAdvance Inc |quote=Takami-Musubi, Kami-Musubi, and Ame-no-Minakanushi are the three gods of creation.}} == History == [[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]] According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|WD=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass|1=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|Shiraiwa Mountain|ja|白岩山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraiwa Mountain|1=shiroiwayama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579633}}, {{ill|Myōhōgatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhōgatake|1=myouhougatake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|WD=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain|1=Mount Kumotori}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]. It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|WD=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Ōshima}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai|1=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kannon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 観音菩薩}} at the site. {{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|WD=Q6443450|lt=Kumano|1=Kumano region}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}. During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. More detailed information on rituals, shrine architecture, and related legends can be found in the full article. == History == === Founding === The shrine's origins trace back to the first century, attributed to the founding by Prince {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a son of the legendary twelfth emperor of Japan, Keikō. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}{{Cite web |title=What is Mitsumine Shrine? |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E5%B3%AF%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE-638822#:~:text=%E3%81%BF%E3%81%A4%E3%81%BF%E3%81%AD%E2%80%90%E3%81%98%E3%82%93%E3%81%98%E3%82%83%E3%80%90%E4%B8%89,%E3%81%91%E3%83%BB%E7%81%AB%E9%99%A4%E3%81%91%E3%81%A8%E3%81%97%E3%81%A6%E6%9C%89%E5%90%8D%E3%80%82 |website=Kotobank |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja |first=Digital Daijisen, Seisenban |last=Japan National Dictionary, Nihon Daihyakka Zensho, Digital Daijisen Plus |publisher=[[DIGITALIO]]}} and is currently listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|WD=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. Together with {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|en|Chichibu Shrine|WD=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine|1=Chichibu Shrine}} and {{ill|Hodosan Shrine|ja|宝登山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hodosan Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寳登山神社}}, it is one of the {{ill|Chichibu Three Shrines|ja|秩父三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135550808|1=Q135550808}}. At the front of the main hall stands a rare {{ill|Mitsu Torii|ja|三ツ鳥居|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsu Torii|1=Mitsutorii|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11354046}}. The shrine worships the {{ill|Japanese wolf|ja|狼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese wolf|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|1=Wolf|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18498}} as a guardian deity[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|WD=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}. == Deities == ; Main Deities * '''{{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi|1=Izanagi}}''' (伊弉諾尊) * '''{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}''' (伊弉册尊) ; Enshrined Deities * {{ill|Zōka Sanshin|ja|造化三神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zōka Sanshin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 別天津神|1=Kotoamatsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q776371}} – {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|WD=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi|1=Ame-no-Minakanushi}}, {{ill|Takami-Musubi|ja|高御産巣日神|1=Takamimusubi|WD=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タカミムスビ}}, and {{ill|Kami-Musubi|ja|神産巣日神|1=Kamimusubi|WD=Q3275901|lt=Kamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カミムスビ}}{{Cite web |title=Ame-no-Minakanushi |url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2038 |website=JapanKnowledge |access-date=2024-12-29 |first=NetAdvance Inc |last=NetAdvance Inc |quote=Takami-Musubi, Kami-Musubi, and Ame-no-Minakanushi are the three gods of creation.}} == History == [[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]] According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|WD=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass|1=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|Shiraiwa Mountain|ja|白岩山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraiwa Mountain|1=shiroiwayama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579633}}, {{ill|Myōhōgatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhōgatake|1=myouhougatake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|WD=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain|1=Mount Kumotori}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]. It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|WD=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Ōshima}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai|1=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kannon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 観音菩薩}} at the site. {{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|WD=Q6443450|lt=Kumano|1=Kumano region}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}. During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. More detailed information on rituals, shrine architecture, and related legends can be found in the full article. == History == === Founding === The shrine's origins trace back to the first century, attributed to the founding by Prince {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a son of the legendary twelfth emperor of Japan, Keikō. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[Category:sn_crud|commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=File:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|prefecture={{ill|Chichibu|WD=Q647079|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}|coordinates={{Coord|35.925431|N|138.930397|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}|deity={{ill|Izanagi and Izanami|WD=Q12259961|1=Izanagi and Izanami}}}}'''Mitsumine Shrine''' is a [[Beppyo Shrine]] in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|en|Chichibu, Saitama|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu, Saitama|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =

Together with {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|en|Chichibu Shrine|WD=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine|1=Chichibu Shrine}} and {{ill|Hodosan Shrine|ja|宝登山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hodosan Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寳登山神社}}, it is one of the {{ill|Chichibu Three Shrines|ja|秩父三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135550808|1=Q135550808}}. At the front of the main hall stands a rare {{ill|Mitsu Torii|ja|三ツ鳥居|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsu Torii|1=Mitsutorii|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11354046}}. The shrine worships the {{ill|Japanese wolf|ja|狼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese wolf|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|1=Wolf|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18498}} as a guardian deity[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|WD=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}. == Deities == ; Main Deities * '''{{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi|1=Izanagi}}''' (伊弉諾尊) * '''{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}''' (伊弉册尊) ; Enshrined Deities * {{ill|Zōka Sanshin|ja|造化三神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zōka Sanshin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 別天津神|1=Kotoamatsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q776371}} – {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|WD=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi|1=Ame-no-Minakanushi}}, {{ill|Takami-Musubi|ja|高御産巣日神|1=Takamimusubi|WD=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タカミムスビ}}, and {{ill|Kami-Musubi|ja|神産巣日神|1=Kamimusubi|WD=Q3275901|lt=Kamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カミムスビ}}{{Cite web |title=Ame-no-Minakanushi |url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2038 |website=JapanKnowledge |access-date=2024-12-29 |first=NetAdvance Inc |last=NetAdvance Inc |quote=Takami-Musubi, Kami-Musubi, and Ame-no-Minakanushi are the three gods of creation.}} == History == [[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]] According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|WD=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass|1=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|Shiraiwa Mountain|ja|白岩山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraiwa Mountain|1=shiroiwayama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579633}}, {{ill|Myōhōgatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhōgatake|1=myouhougatake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|WD=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain|1=Mount Kumotori}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]. It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|WD=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Ōshima}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai|1=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kannon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 観音菩薩}} at the site. {{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|WD=Q6443450|lt=Kumano|1=Kumano region}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}. During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. More detailed information on rituals, shrine architecture, and related legends can be found in the full article. == History == === Founding === The shrine's origins trace back to the first century, attributed to the founding by Prince {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a son of the legendary twelfth emperor of Japan, Keikō. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[Category:sn_crud|commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=File:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|prefecture={{ill|Chichibu|WD=Q647079|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}|coordinates={{Coord|35.925431|N|138.930397|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}|deity={{ill|Izanagi and Izanami|WD=Q12259961|1=Izanagi and Izanami}}}}'''Mitsumine Shrine''' is a [[Beppyo Shrine]] in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|en|Chichibu, Saitama|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu, Saitama|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =

It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}{{Cite web |title=What is Mitsumine Shrine? |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E5%B3%AF%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE-638822#:~:text=%E3%81%BF%E3%81%A4%E3%81%BF%E3%81%AD%E2%80%90%E3%81%98%E3%82%93%E3%81%98%E3%82%83%E3%80%90%E4%B8%89,%E3%81%91%E3%83%BB%E7%81%AB%E9%99%A4%E3%81%91%E3%81%A8%E3%81%97%E3%81%A6%E6%9C%89%E5%90%8D%E3%80%82 |website=Kotobank |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja |first=Digital Daijisen, Seisenban |last=Japan National Dictionary, Nihon Daihyakka Zensho, Digital Daijisen Plus |publisher=[[DIGITALIO]]}} and is currently listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|WD=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. Together with {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|en|Chichibu Shrine|WD=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine|1=Chichibu Shrine}} and {{ill|Hodosan Shrine|ja|宝登山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hodosan Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寳登山神社}}, it is one of the {{ill|Chichibu Three Shrines|ja|秩父三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135550808|1=Q135550808}}. At the front of the main hall stands a rare {{ill|Mitsu Torii|ja|三ツ鳥居|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsu Torii|1=Mitsutorii|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11354046}}. The shrine worships the {{ill|Japanese wolf|ja|狼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese wolf|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|1=Wolf|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18498}} as a guardian deity[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|WD=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}. == Deities == ; Main Deities * '''{{ill|Izanagi|en|Izanagi|WD=Q813858|lt=Izanagi|1=Izanagi}}''' (伊弉諾尊) * '''{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}''' (伊弉册尊) ; Enshrined Deities * {{ill|Zōka Sanshin|ja|造化三神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zōka Sanshin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 別天津神|1=Kotoamatsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q776371}} – {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|WD=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi|1=Ame-no-Minakanushi}}, {{ill|Takami-Musubi|ja|高御産巣日神|1=Takamimusubi|WD=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タカミムスビ}}, and {{ill|Kami-Musubi|ja|神産巣日神|1=Kamimusubi|WD=Q3275901|lt=Kamimusubi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kami-Musubi|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamimusubi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カミムスビ}}{{Cite web |title=Ame-no-Minakanushi |url=https://japanknowledge.com/introduction/keyword.html?i=2038 |website=JapanKnowledge |access-date=2024-12-29 |first=NetAdvance Inc |last=NetAdvance Inc |quote=Takami-Musubi, Kami-Musubi, and Ame-no-Minakanushi are the three gods of creation.}} == History == [[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]] According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|WD=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass|1=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|Shiraiwa Mountain|ja|白岩山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraiwa Mountain|1=shiroiwayama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579633}}, {{ill|Myōhōgatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhōgatake|1=myouhougatake|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|WD=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain|1=Mount Kumotori}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]. It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|WD=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Ōshima}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai|1=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kannon|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 観音菩薩}} at the site. {{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|WD=Q6443450|lt=Kumano|1=Kumano region}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}. During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. More detailed information on rituals, shrine architecture, and related legends can be found in the full article. == History == === Founding === The shrine's origins trace back to the first century, attributed to the founding by Prince {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a son of the legendary twelfth emperor of Japan, Keikō. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[Category:sn_crud|commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=File:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|prefecture={{ill|Chichibu|WD=Q647079|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}|coordinates={{Coord|35.925431|N|138.930397|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}|deity={{ill|Izanagi and Izanami|WD=Q12259961|1=Izanagi and Izanami}}}}'''Mitsumine Shrine''' is a [[Beppyo Shrine]] in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|en|Chichibu, Saitama|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu, Saitama|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =
Haiden

Setsubun Exorcism Festival ("Gomottomo-sama," {{ill|February 3|en|February 3|WD=Q2315|lt=February 3|1=February 3}}) | map = Japan Saitama }} [[File:Mitsumine Shrine - various scenes - Feb 3 2021.webm|thumb|Mitsumine Shrine]] '''Mitsumine Shrine''' (三峯神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|ja|埼玉県秩父市|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu, Saitama|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}{{Cite web |title=What is Mitsumine Shrine? |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E5%B3%AF%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE-638822#:~:text=%E3%81%BF%E3%81%A4%E3%81%BF%E3%81%AD%E2%80%90%E3%81%98%E3%82%93%E3%81%98%E3%82%83%E3%80%90%E4%B8%89,%E3%81%91%E3%83%BB%E7%81%AB%E9%99%A4%E3%81%91%E3%81%A8%E3%81%97%E3%81%A6%E6%9C%89%E5%90%8D%E3%80%82 |website=Kotobank |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja |first=Digital Daijisen, Seisenban |last=Japan National Dictionary, Nihon Daihyakka Zensho, Digital Daijisen Plus |publisher=[[DIGITALIO]]}} and is currently listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|WD=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. Together with {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|en|Chichibu Shrine|WD=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine|1=Chichibu Shrine}} and {{ill|Hodosan Shrine|ja|宝登山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hodosan Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 寳登山神社}}, it is one of the {{ill|Chichibu Three Shrines|ja|秩父三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chichibu Three Shrines|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|WD=Q135550808|1=Q135550808}}. At the front of the main hall stands a rare {{ill|Mitsu Torii|ja|三ツ鳥居|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mitsu Torii|1=Mitsutorii|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11354046}}. The shrine worships the {{ill|Japanese wolf|ja|狼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese wolf|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|1=Wolf|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q18498}} as a guardian deity[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|WD=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}. == Deities == ; During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}} === Development and Decline === Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|WD=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja|1=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine. The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords. === Restoration and Modern Era === A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002. == Cultural and Spiritual Significance == Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site. As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}} ==Gallery== File:Chichibu Touryuubasi Bridge from below.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi 1 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge from above.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi 2 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi 3.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi 3 File:Chichibu Touryuubasi bridge looking away from shrine.jpg|alt=秩父投龍橋 4|Chichibu Touryuubasi 4 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine starting from the street.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 1|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 1 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the highway.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 2|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 2 File:Mitsumine Shrine approach looking towards the Shrine.jpg|alt=投龍橋取付道路 3|Chichibu Touryuubasi Toritukedouro 3 File:Detailed sculptures of animals and nature in a shinto shrine on the Mt.Kumotori, Japan.jpg|alt=熊取山の神社にある動物と自然の詳細な彫刻|Detailed sculptures at a Shinto shrine on Mt. [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[co:commons:Category:Mitsumine-jinja]][[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] [[fr:Mitsumine-jinja]][[ja:三峯神社]][[simple:Mitsumine Shrine]] {{infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|image=File:Mitsumine-jinja, Haiden.jpg|prefecture={{ill|Chichibu|WD=Q647079|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}|coordinates={{Coord|35.925431|N|138.930397|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}|deity={{ill|Izanagi and Izanami|WD=Q12259961|1=Izanagi and Izanami}}}}'''Mitsumine Shrine''' is a [[Beppyo Shrine]] in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|en|Chichibu, Saitama|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu, Saitama|1=Chichibu, Saitama}}. It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Power spot (spirituality)|qq=}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}} ==Overview== {{otheruses|A Shinto shrine in Chichibu, Saitama Prefecture|A shrine in Setagaya, Tokyo|Mitsumine Shrine (Setagaya, Kinuta)}} {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mitsumine Shrine | image =
Haiden

{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} (伊弉册尊) | shrine_Rank = Former {{ill|Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja|県社|1=Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|WD=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prefectural shrine (Japan)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近代社格制度|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q712534}}
